summary: Merge sort is a stable divide-and-conquer sort: split the array in half, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves. It guarantees O(n log n) time in every case at the cost of O(n) extra space.

sections.heading: The three steps
bullets: Divide: split the array at the middle.
Conquer: recursively sort each half (a single element is already sorted).
Combine: merge the two sorted halves into one sorted run.
sections.code:
sort(a, lo, hi):
  if hi - lo < 2: return
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2
  sort(a, lo, mid); sort(a, mid, hi)
  merge(a, lo, mid, hi)

sections.heading: The merge procedure
sections.body: Walk both halves with two indexes, always copying the smaller front element to a temporary buffer; when one side is exhausted copy the rest. Taking from the left half on ties keeps equal elements in their original order, which makes the sort stable.

sections.heading: Walkthrough
sections.body: [38, 27, 43, 10] splits into [38, 27] and [43, 10], then into singletons. Merging gives [27, 38] and [10, 43], and the final merge produces [10, 27, 38, 43].

sections.heading: Complexity
bullets: Time: O(n log n) best, average, and worst: log n levels, O(n) merging per level.
Space: O(n) for the temporary buffer (plus O(log n) recursion).
Not in place, and not adaptive in the basic form.

sections.heading: Strengths and weaknesses
bullets: Excellent for linked lists (merging needs no extra array) and for external sorting of data larger than memory.
Parallelizes naturally, since halves are independent.
Slower than quick sort on arrays in practice because of the copying and extra memory traffic.

sections.body: Start with runs of length 1 and repeatedly merge adjacent runs, doubling the run length each pass (1, 2, 4, ...). Same O(n log n), but no call stack and easy to adapt for linked lists and external files.

An inversion is a pair i < j with a[i] > a[j]. During a merge, when an element from the right half is taken before remaining left elements, it forms inversions with all of them. Summing these counts inversions in O(n log n), versus O(n²) by brute force.
Find the middle with fast/slow pointers, split, recursively sort both halves, and merge by relinking nodes. Space is O(log n) for recursion only, and this is the standard way to sort a linked list.
Sort chunks that fit in memory, write them as sorted runs to disk, then k-way merge the runs with a heap, reading each run sequentially. This is how databases sort huge tables.

subtopics.title: Timsort
subtopics.summary: Merge sort in the real world.

sections.body: Python and Java use Timsort: it finds naturally ordered runs, extends short ones with insertion sort, and merges them with galloping. It is stable and runs in O(n) on already sorted data.

takeaways: Split, sort halves, merge: O(n log n) always.
Stable and predictable, but needs O(n) extra space.
Ideal for linked lists and external sorting.
Merging counts inversions as a by-product.
